title: Nodes, antinodes and wavelength
prior_knowledge_summary: Students can explain stationary-wave formation and identify fixed nodes and antinodes across time.
new_learning: Use repeated node or antinode positions to determine wavelength.

visual_rules.style: colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch on rectangular white paper

blocks.title: How much wave fits between fixed points?
content: A stationary-wave picture shows fixed nodes, but no wavelength arrow. Can the node pattern reveal the wavelength?
The repeated pattern provides a built-in ruler.

figure.purpose: Pose wavelength measurement from a stationary pattern.
figure.brief: White-paper string sketch with four nodes and three loops; ask where one wavelength fits without giving the answer.
figure.alt_text: A stationary wave with several fixed nodes.

blocks.title: One loop is half a wavelength
content: Adjacent nodes bound one loop. Moving from one node to the next changes the component-wave phase by half a cycle, so adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart.
Adjacent antinodes are also half a wavelength apart. A node to its nearest antinode is half of that distance, one quarter wavelength.

figure.purpose: Connect loop geometry to wavelength fractions.
figure.brief: Label adjacent nodes N1,N2 and an intervening antinode A; show N1-N2 as lambda/2 and N1-A as lambda/4.
figure.alt_text: Node and antinode spacing marked as fractions of wavelength.

blocks.title: Formula to remember
content: Here d is the distance in metres and lambda is wavelength in metres.
Choose the relation that matches the two positions actually measured. Do not use lambda/4 for two adjacent nodes.

figure.purpose: Provide a comparison reference for the three spacings.
figure.brief: Three aligned mini-sketches: node-node, antinode-antinode, nearest node-antinode with matching symbolic distances.

blocks.title: From adjacent nodes to wavelength
content: Two adjacent nodes are 7.5 cm apart. Since d = lambda/2, lambda = 2d = 15.0 cm = 0.150 m.
Check: half of 15.0 cm is 7.5 cm, so the spacing returns the measurement.

figure.purpose: Model unit-safe reverse use of the spacing formula.
figure.brief: Annotated working layout with 7.5 cm node spacing, lambda=2d, 15.0 cm and conversion to 0.150 m.
figure.alt_text: A worked node-spacing calculation gives wavelength.

blocks.title: Measure several gaps for a better result
content: If the distance from the first to the sixth node is 40.0 cm, there are five node-to-node gaps, not six. Each gap is lambda/2.
So one gap is 40.0/5 = 8.00 cm and lambda = 16.0 cm. Measuring several gaps reduces the percentage effect of position-reading uncertainty.

figure.purpose: Teach interval counting and multi-gap measurement.
figure.brief: Number six nodes and bracket five intervals across 40.0 cm; keep final wavelength off the figure.
figure.alt_text: Six nodes define five equal node-to-node intervals.

blocks.title: Name, count, calculate, check
content: First name the two marked positions. Then count intervals between them. Choose lambda/2 or lambda/4, calculate with consistent units, and check by substituting back.
A common error is counting marked nodes instead of gaps. Four nodes contain three adjacent-node gaps.

figure.purpose: Summarise a reliable spacing method and interval-count correction.
figure.brief: Four-box flow with a small four-node, three-gap correction sketch.
figure.alt_text: A four-step method for stationary-wave spacing problems.

misconceptions_addressed: Adjacent nodes are one wavelength apart.
skills_students_can_now_use: Determine wavelength from node or antinode positions.
Convert spacing units and check results.
next_lesson_can_assume: Nodes and antinodes are fixed and alternated by lambda/4.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: experimental procedures for strings, air columns or microwaves
